summary_html: Child safely **reunified with parent or guardian**, case closed. Federal policy treats reunification as the preferred outcome once risk factors are mitigated.
authority_html:
- **Adoption and Safe Families Act (ASFA)** — establishes reunification timelines and permanency goals  
- **SSA Title IV-E (42 U.S.C. §§ 670–679c)** — funds reunification services and tracks permanency outcomes

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: May v. Harrison County Department of Human Services
key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed the youth court's termination of a mother's parental rights, holding the clear-and-convincing burden had been satisfied and rejecting her argument that durable legal custody should have been ordered instead.
key_cases.relevance: The opinion canvasses the Adoption and Safe Families Act's limits on required reunification efforts in aggravated-circumstances cases.
key_cases.quote: The burden of proof in order to establish a case for termination of parental rights is clear and convincing evidence.

key_cases.holding: Reviewing the statute de novo, the Court reversed a youth court's bypass of reunification, holding that Section 43-21-603(7)(c) requires both one of the three enumerated criteria and a best-interest finding, and that a father's pre-birth criminal history was not conduct to which he subjected the child.
key_cases.relevance: The most recent Mississippi authority protecting the reunification track from being bypassed on loose 'aggravated circumstances' reasoning.
key_cases.quote: after determining that one of the first three criteria have been met, the youth court must also determine that bypassing reunification is in the best interests of the child

key_cases.case_name: G.Q.A. v. Harrison County Department of Human Services
key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed a family court judgment terminating both parents' rights to a severely burned and malnourished child, holding that family court terminations are reviewed under the same clear-and-convincing standard as chancery terminations and that the findings of serial abuse and substantial erosion of the relationship were supported by substantial evidence.
key_cases.relevance: Sets out the Adoption and Safe Families Act provision that reasonable efforts to reunite are not required once a court finds the parent subjected the child to aggravated circumstances - the federal limit on the reunification track that May later applies.
key_cases.quote: A Family Court judgment concerning termination of parental rights will be reviewed under the same standard as a Chancery Court judgment, which is clear and convincing evidence.

key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed the youth court's grant of durable legal custody of a chronically abused child to her long-time foster parents, but reversed the portion of the judgment permanently relieving the Department of Human Services of any further involvement, holding that durable legal custody leaves the parents' residual rights intact and ends only the mandatory annual dispositional reviews, not the youth court's jurisdiction or the Department's ability to monitor.
key_cases.relevance: Reunification may be set aside in favour of durable legal custody where the youth court determines on the evidence before it that returning the child is not in her best interest.
key_cases.quote: The fact that under durable legal custody the parent retains some form of residual rights and responsibilities is a vital and obvious distinction to termination of parental rights.

key_cases.case_name: In the Matter of the Dissolution of the Marriage of Leverock and Hamby: Pendleton v. Leverock
key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed the chancellor's refusal to terminate the father's parental rights but reversed the award of custody to him, holding the record established desertion so that the natural-parent presumption was rebutted and custody had to be redetermined through an on-the-record Albright best-interests analysis.
key_cases.relevance: Return to the natural parent does not follow automatically from a refusal to terminate; a parent who deserted the child loses the presumptive claim to custody.
key_cases.quote: This presumption in favor of a natural parent has long been recognized, and Tony is entitled to it unless there is proof that he has relinquished it.

extended_foster_care_age: To 20 under youth court jurisdiction (Miss. Code § 43-21-151(2)); to 21 only if MDCPS petitions the chancery court before the 20th birthday (MDCPS Foster Care Policy, Section D, F. Custody Beyond Age 20)

Santosky v. Kramer standard not met
